newsitem.title: UK: Eurobonds see couple ground-breaking transactions.
newsitem.headline: Eurobonds see couple ground-breaking transactions.

text.p: ** The primary market saw two ground-breaking transactions
on Tuesday. Siemens became the first company to launch a
Eurobond which can be redenominated in euros post-EMU.
Fannie Mae set the first stg-denominated global bond.
** Other activity in the French franc sector included a 2.0
billion FFR 12-year offering for Abbey National and a 1.5
billion 10-year deal for Alcatel.
** Ukraine was reported to be planning its debut Eurobond.
All three deals, each paying a coupon of 5.50 percent, will be redenominated in euros after EMU, after which they will be fungible and merged to create a jumbo euro Eurobond.

J.P. Morgan said distribution of the deals was broad with a strong bid for the mark tranche from London, Switzerland and into Germany, France, Benelux, Austria, Italy, and the Middle and Far East. Paribas said one-third of the French franc paper sold to French institutional investors, with the rest selling to Asian and European investors. ABN AMRO syndicate manager said 75 percent of the guilder paper went to Dutch institutional investors with the rest being sold to European institutions.

Syndicate managers at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (joint lead manager on all tranches), Paribas (joint lead on the French franc tranche) and ABN AMRO Hoare Govett (joint lead on the guilder tranche) praised the deal.
Siemens now becomes the first company to prepare its international long-term debt for a single European currency.
"The scarcity value, the magic triple-A for a corporate and the euro fungibility clause are all the right components to make it a tremendous success," a Paribas syndicate manager said.
Also making new inroads was the launch of the first-ever sterling-denominated Eurobond for Fannie Mae via joint lead managers BZW and Merrill Lynch.
The 1.0 billion stg June 2002 bond will be priced on Wednesday to yield 10 basis points over the 7.00 percent British government bond (gilt) due June 2002.
The lead managers could not comment on the issue prior to its pricing due to U.S. SEC regulations, they said.

Syndicate sources away from the leads said there had been heavy demand from British institutional accounts. Japan has a public holiday -- National Foundation Day -- but investors are expected to purchase paper overnight.
"The deal is being marketed as a surrogate gilt," a dealer said, adding Fannie Mae had probably been attracted by arbitrage opportunities in the sector.
Traders said sterling benefits from its status as a "safe haven" currency, unlikely to join European economic and monetary union at the outset.
-- Hayley Pienaar, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7718
